Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI.

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them once and for all. Keep refactoring of individual examples minimal: prefer configuration- and setup-level changes — adding tags, restructuring shared setup, wrapping execution. What the examples assert must stay the same. No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

Only `rspec spec/<some-folder>`. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. In the end, we want these two groups together to run at least twice as fast as they do today. Store any insights/comments/plans (such as baseline metrics) that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

We anticipate a similar speed-up of >30% compared to the baseline (captured at the previous step, before any optimization work). Note that optimizations made for models could have already improved requests specs enough. If that's the case, look for request-specific bottlenecks to get the rest of the way there.

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output_head": "# RSpec Test Suite Optimization Notes & Plan

## Overview

Goal: Significantly reduce sequential RSpec runtime (targeting >= 2x speedup across `spec/models` + `spec/requests` combined) via profiling-driven, configuration- and setup-level optimizations without altering what examples assert or changing application runtime behavior.

---

## Phase 1: `spec/models`

### Baseline Metrics (before any changes)

Command: `bundle exec rspec spec/models --format progress --profile 20`

- **Examples:** 1,795 examples, 0 failures (152 spec files)
- **Wall time (clean run, seed `18019`):** `120.2s` (`real 2m1.989s`, `user 1m48.572s`, `sys 0m3.826s`)
- **SQL queries (`EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record`):** 113,955 queries (`21.57s` DB/AR event time; `33.4%` of total wall time in `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql`!)
- **Inline Sidekiq jobs (`EVENT_PROF=sidekiq.inline`):** 3,908 jobs (`36.20s`, `26.7%` of profiled run)
- **Fabrication (`FPROF=1`):** 4,721 fabricated objects (3,243 top-level), `120.61s` of `137.61s` (`87.6%`)
  - `account`: 1,194 calls (`30.77s`, `25.8ms`/call)
  - `bookmark`: 1,019 calls (only 17 top-level; `32.96s`, `32.3ms`/call)
  - `status`: 1,003 calls (`64.25s`, `64.1ms`/call)
  - `login_activity`: 270 calls (0 top-level; `0.93s`)
  - `user`: 93 calls (`3.51s`, `37.7ms`/call)
- **RSpecDissect (`RD_PROF=1`):** `118.11s` setup time out of `142.72s` (`82.7%` spent in setup!)
- **Test log output (`log/test.log`):** ~32 MB written per `spec/models` run

### Key Profiling Findings (StackProf + TestProf)

1. **Global `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` leak (~29.0% of total runtime, ~35s):**
   - `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb:6` contained leftover debug code (`ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true`) directly inside `RSpec.describe`, executing at file-load time and enabling backtrace capture + `Rails::BacktraceCleaner` for every SQL query in the entire RSpec process (affecting all spec directories whenever that file was loaded).
   - StackProf showed `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#log_query_source` at `29.0%` of total samples (`BacktraceCleaner#first_clean_frame` `28.5%`, `Rails::BacktraceCleaner#initialize` `3.5%`).

2. **Debug-level logging in test environment (~4.4% of total runtime, ~5-6s + 32 MB/run disk I/O):**
   - `config/environments/test.rb` left `config.log_level` at default `:debug`, causing `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` to format/colorize/filter bind parameters for >100k SQL queries and write ~32 MB per run to `log/test.log`.
   - Verified no spec in `spec/` depends on `Rails.logger.level == :debug` (`spec/models/concerns/remotable_spec.rb` stubs `Rails.logger.debug` directly).

3. **Global `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` executing `TriggerWebhookWorker` on every record creation (~24.1% of baseline / ~35-42% post-logging):**
   - `spec/rails_helper.rb` forced `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` before every example.
   - `TriggerWebhookWorker#perform` accounted for 94%+ of inline Sidekiq runtime (`34,486` / `36,608` Sidekiq samples): on every `User`, `Status`, `Account`, or `Report` creation, `WebhookService#call` serialized the entire `REST::Admin::WebhookEventSerializer` JSON payload (issuing extra queries for `email`, `ip`, `role`, `account_stat`, `followers_count`) before checking `Webhook.enabled` (which was empty) and discarding the result.
   - Across all 1,795 model examples, only **3 spec files** (4 examples) actually depended on inline Sidekiq execution (all 4 using `capture_emails` for `deliver_later` via ActiveJob/Sidekiq).

4. **Repeated database setup in slow model specs (~80.8% setup time after Tier 1):**
   - Even after fixing logging and Sidekiq, `RSpecDissect` showed `39.8s` of `49.2s` spent in setup (`4,721` fabricated records), heavily concentrated in ~20 model spec files recreating identical sets of statuses, accounts, tags, notifications, and policies before every example.

5. **Remaining irreducible / Phase 3 costs:**
   - `spec/models/media_attachment_spec.rb` (~5.0s) runs real libvips/ffmpeg media processing across 14 media fixture formats (`IO.select` / `Terrapin` ~3.8s, `boop.mp3` cover art ~2.6s).
   - First-example route loading (`Rails.application.reload_routes_unless_loaded` in `spec/rails_helper.rb`) adds ~0.4s once per process.
   - Factory cascades & BCrypt hashing (see Phase 3 notes below).

### Changes Applied in Phase 1

1. **Systemic / Configuration-level changes:**
   - Removed leaked `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` from `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`.
   - Set `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'warn')` in `config/environments/test.rb` (matches `production.rb` pattern; developers can still pass `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`).
   - Added `require 'test_prof/recipes/rspec/let_it_be'` in `spec/rails_helper.rb`.
   - Switched `Sidekiq.testing!` default for `type: :model` to `:fake` (including `before(:context, type: :model)` so `before_all`/`let_it_be` run in `:fake` mode, and `after(:each, :side",
  "output_tail": "y `AccountStat` / `StatusStat` associations:**
   - Mastodon creates `AccountStat` rows lazily (e.g., when a `Follow` or `Status` is created inside an example). If an `Account` created in `let_it_be` doesn't have an `AccountStat` yet, Example 1 creates and caches one on the Ruby object, Example 1 rolls back the DB transaction, and Example 2 crashes with `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound: Couldn't find AccountStat`.
   - **Rule:** Always pass `refind: true` (or `reload: true`) on `let_it_be` `Account` / `Status` records that may be followed, mutated, or have statuses/reactions created for them inside examples.

2. **Redis and `Rails.cache` are cleared after every example:**
   - `spec/rails_helper.rb` runs `Rails.cache.clear` and `redis.del(redis.keys)` in `config.after`.
   - **Rule:** Never rely on Redis keys (e.g., `AccountStatusesCleanupPolicy#record_last_inspected`, `Trends::Statuses#add`) or `Rails.cache` entries created in `before_all` persisting past Example 1. Keep Redis setup in `before(:each)` while keeping PostgreSQL records in `let_it_be` / `before_all`.

3. **Memoized ivars on AR models (e.g., `Collection#items_for`):**
   - Use `refind: true` rather than `reload: true` when an example asserts on memoization or mutates associations like `account.user`.

4. **`Setting.*` writes and `Sidekiq.testing!` inside `before_all`:**
   - `config.before(:context, type: :model)` ensures `before_all` runs with `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` even if a preceding example used `:inline`. When extending `:fake` to `type: :request`, include `:request` in the same `before(:context)` hook.

---

## Plan for Future Phases

### Phase 2: `spec/requests`

1. **Capture clean baseline** of `bundle exec rspec spec/requests` plus `FPROF=1`, `RD_PROF=1`, `EVENT_PROF="sql.active_record,sidekiq.inline,process_action.action_controller"`, and `TEST_STACK_PROF=1`.
   - Note: `spec/requests` already benefits from Phase 1's `verbose_query_logs` fix and `config.log_level = 'warn'`!
2. **Switch `type: :request` to `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` by default with `:sidekiq_inline` tag:**
   - Request specs create many users/accounts/statuses and currently run `TriggerWebhookWorker` and other workers inline on every creation.
   - Audit which request specs genuinely require inline Sidekiq (e.g., `capture_emails`, worker side-effects asserted directly after HTTP request) and tag them `:sidekiq_inline`.
3. **Audit request-specific setup bottlenecks:**
   - Check Devise `sign_in` (note `spec/rails_helper.rb` monkey-patches `sign_in` to create `SessionActivation` rows), OAuth `Doorkeeper::AccessToken` / `Doorkeeper::Application` fabrication, and repeated `user` / `account` / `status` setup across request spec files.
   - Apply `let_it_be` / `before_all` to the slowest request spec suites identified by `RD_PROF=1`.
   - Check ActionView / asset / HAML / Vite / middleware overhead via StackProf (e.g., `config.action_view.annotate_rendered_view_with_filenames`, Rack::Attack, etc.).

### Phase 3: Fabricators (`spec/fabricators/`) — Do Not Touch Until Factories Phase

Profiling `spec/models` uncovered massive hidden cascades inside `spec/fabricators/` that affect **all** spec types:

1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb:11` (HUGE):**
   ```ruby
   after_create do |status|
     Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status)
   end
   ```
   - Every `Fabricate(:status)` creates an unexpected `Bookmark`, which via `bookmark_fabricator.rb` builds a brand-new `Account` -> builds a brand-new `User` -> hashes a BCrypt password -> creates 2 `LoginActivity` rows!
   - Even after Phase 1 `let_it_be` reductions, `bookmark` accounted for `449` calls (`5.41s`, ~19% of remaining factory time in `spec/models`!).
   - Removing this implicit `after_create` (and adding explicit `Fabricate(:bookmark)` only in the few specs that actually expect a bookmark) will yield another huge suite-wide speedup.

2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb:17`:**
   ```ruby
   after_create do |user|
     2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) }
   end
   ```
   - Creates 2 `LoginActivity` rows for every fabricated `User` (including every local `Account`!). Most specs never inspect `login_activities`.

3. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb:11` (BCrypt hashing):**
   - `password '123456789'` runs `BCrypt::Password.create` (cost 4) on every fabricated `User` / local `Account` (~3.3s in `spec/models` at baseline; likely much higher in `spec/requests`!).
   - Precomputing a single static `Devise::Encryptor.digest(User, '123456789')` and assigning `encrypted_password` directly (unless `:password` is explicitly passed) will eliminate almost all BCrypt CPU time across the entire suite.

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "post #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date', 'Digest')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end
end

steps.reasoning_content:
**My Immediate Assessment: Code Red! Performance Catastrophe Detected!**

OH. MY. GOD. Stop everything! I need to document this discovery. These numbers are screaming at me. We have some serious bottlenecks here. Let's break it down:

First, this routing issue with `ActionDispatch::Routing::RouteSet` is a major red flag. Specifically, `define_url_helper` and `clear!` are dominating. We're seeing *thousands* of self-samples in `define_method` and `remove_method` related to route definition and clearing. This indicates that we're reloading routes far too often. I need to dive in and identify precisely what's calling `reload_routes!`, `define_url_helper`, and `clear!` and where these calls originate. This could be a major source of CPU churn, particularly given the magnitude of the samples. I need to run a script against the StackProf dump to cleanly categorize the major areas of impact.

Second, the `Sidekiq::Job::Setter#perform_async` usage within `spec/requests` is staggering. Over *30%* of the total time! Even more alarming is what's *inside* `perform_async`: `WebhookService#serialize_event` and `User#trigger_webhooks`, which are taking up significant time as well. This inline Sidekiq usage, especially for potentially IO-bound operations, could be devastating for test performance. I need to evaluate if these Sidekiq jobs are truly necessary to run synchronously in these specs.

Third, `Object#Fabricate` is absolutely eating our lunch, accounting for an astounding *64.78%* of `spec/requests`. This is just insane. We're spending far more time constructing test data than we are actually *testing* the application logic. And get this: the actual HTTP requests (`ActionDispatch::Integration::Session#process`) are only 14%! This means, out of the total time in `spec/requests`, only about 21 seconds are for the actual HTTP requests, the rest is eaten by overhead, like `Fabricate`, route reloading, and Sidekiq! This is an enormous opportunity for optimization. We need to explore strategies for reducing `Fabricate` usage. Could we use factory caching, more efficient factories, or even pre-built test fixtures?

Fourth, and as a specific indicator of the problem is the fact that `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` alone accounts for 20.6% of the samples.

My immediate next steps are clear:

1.  Identify the root cause of the `ActionDispatch::Routing::RouteSet` churn and mitigate the route reloading.
2.  Assess the necessity of synchronous Sidekiq jobs in these tests and explore asynchronous execution where possible.
3.  Critically review the `Fabricate` usage in the tests and find ways to significantly reduce it. I'm thinking factory caching or fixture alternatives.

This is a serious performance bottleneck. We're spending an obscene amount of time on test setup. Let's fix it!

require "stackprof"
data = Marshal.load(File.binread("tmp/test_prof/requests-baseline-wall.dump"))

frames.select { |f| f[:file].to_s.include?("/app/workers/") }.sort_by { |f| -f[:total_samples] }.first(25).each do |f|
  pct = (f[:total_samples] / total * 100).round(2)
  printf "%6.2f%% %7d  %s  [%s:%s]\n", pct, f[:total_samples], f[:name], f[:file].to_s.sub(Dir.pwd + "/", ""), f[:line]
end

puts "\n=== Top spec/requests files (max frame per file) ==="
by_file = frames.select { |f| f[:file].to_s.include?("spec/requests/") }.group_by { |f| f[:file].sub(Dir.pwd + "/", "") }
by_file.map { |file, fs| [file, fs.map { |f| f[:total_samples] }.max] }.sort_by { |_, s| -s }.first(35).each do |file, s|
  printf "%6.2f%% %7d  %s\n", (s / total * 100), s, file
end
'

steps.reasoning_content:
**Analysis of Request Spec Performance Bottlenecks**

Okay, this is fantastic! StackProf has really delivered the goods. I'm looking at the results for the request specs, and it's crystal clear where the major bottlenecks are.

First of all, and this is huge, the pervasive use of `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` in the request specs is a massive drag. It's taking up over 30% of the entire `spec/requests` suite! Specifically, `TriggerWebhookWorker#perform`, `LocalNotificationWorker#perform`, `DistributionWorker#perform`, and several others are the main culprits. This is costing us roughly 46 seconds of execution time. This has to be addressed.

Second, the `signature_verification_spec.rb` (and possibly `csp_spec.rb`) is calling `Rails.application.reload_routes!` thirty times – once per example. This single method call is eating up ~4% of the time, or around 7.3 seconds, just reloading the routes! I need to investigate whether this is happening in other specs too and see if there is an alternative strategy.

Third, `spec/support/api_authentication.rb` and `spec/support/examples/api.rb` are proving to be another major source of slowdown. Creating new `user`, `application`, and `access_token` objects for *every* example in dozens of API spec files is clearly inefficient. `Fabricate` is being called excessively in `api_authentication.rb` . With these numbers, switching to `let_it_be` or re-evaluating the authentication setup in those support files could potentially give us a significant speed boost across a large number of request specs with just one change.

Next, a single file, `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`, is consuming a staggering 20.6% of the total time (27.65 seconds for just 258 examples). This needs immediate attention. I'm going to dig into the code of that spec right away.

Finally, there are other individual specs like `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`, and `spec/requests/activitypub/contexts_spec.rb` that are contributing significant overhead. **Performance Optimization Opportunities in Mastodon's Testing Suite**

Okay, here's what's going through my mind as I dig into these specs. First, I'm looking at `signature_verification_spec.rb`. It's screaming at me! I see that every single one of its 30 examples is needlessly running `Rails.application.routes.draw { ... }` in a `before` block. This destroys and *recreates* all ~500 Mastodon routes, followed by `Rails.application.reload_routes!` which does the same! Thirty times! That's insane. This is costing us big time – 7.33 seconds for a spec that should take closer to 0.3 seconds. We can drastically improve this by drawing the test routes *once* in a `before(:all)` (or `before(:context)`) block and reloading them *once* in an `after(:all)` block. We can keep the `stub_const('ActivityPub::TestsController', ...)` per-example (or in `before(:each)`). This is a standard pattern for RSpec mocks anyway, since `stub_const` resets between examples. Or, even better, we should explore if `Rails.application.routes.append` is an option and doesn't destroy existing routes. With this, the spec will drop to around ~0.4 seconds – huge win! I also realized this approach is perfectly isolated to this specific `describe` block.

Now, looking deeper, I'm going to apply this same pattern to `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb` – is that `stub_const` called per example? Yes, the RSpec mocks behavior confirms it. It looks like it is, so we can draw the routes once and reload them once. Also, I see `actor_keypair` is parsed via `OpenSSL::PKey.read` on every example. steps.reasoning_content:
**Analyzing the StackProf Results**

Okay, here's what I'm seeing from this StackProf data – and it's quite interesting. First off, wow, look at the details we uncovered!

I have to start with `Premailer::Adapter::Nokogiri#to_inline_css` at 1.76%, with over three thousand samples! I suspect it's likely being called in Sidekiq, probably during email sending related to user or notification creation. Time to go dig into that.

Now, this `RedisClient#pipelined` at a whopping 30.19% – that's a red flag. Digging deeper, it looks like `Sidekiq::Middleware::Chain#invoke` is responsible, sitting at 30.16%. It seems that `Sidekiq::Client#raw_push` wraps `Sidekiq::TestingClient#atomic_push` inside `conn.pipelined`. I need to confirm this connection.

Then we have `spec/support/api_authentication.rb`, which is used in 71 spec files. That file is responsible for 5.97% and 5.59% with `user` and `token` respectively! Wait a second. Since `token` calls `user` to get `resource_owner_id`, it seems that `user` is counted inside `token`, but then, `user` is at `11,326` samples, `headers` is `10,682` and `token` is `10,603`. Why is `user` slightly larger than `headers`? Because some specs access `user` directly without `headers` or `user` is accessed first before `headers`. Regardless, it's accounting for roughly 6-10% of the entire spec suite! That's something to investigate for sure.

I took a quick look at `rails_helper.rb` – the cache clearing on line 144 (`Rails.cache.clear; redis.del(redis.keys)`) is only 0.19%, so negligible, though `redis.flushdb` could be a cleaner alternative if needed. And the DNS stubbing on line 129 is even smaller.

Finally, the big hitters: `ActiveRecord::Base#save` / `Fabricate` is a massive 64.78%, and `Sidekiq` is also sitting at 30.53%. Obviously, those are expected, but worth noting.

I need to confirm these things. I'm going to re-run the StackProf focusing on `Premailer::Adapter::Nokogiri#to_inline_css` and `RedisClient#pipelined` to get a clearer picture of their call chains and confirm what's going on.

It's a noticeable win, and even better, once we refactor those `before` blocks to `before_all` in Tier 2, we'll see further improvement. Specifically, I'll be searching for `capture_emails`, `ActionMailer::Base.deliveries`, `deliveries`, `Worker`, `perform_async`, `Sidekiq`, `have_enqueued`, and `have_received`. steps.reasoning_content:
**Deep Dive into `spec/requests` Performance**

Okay, so I've been digging into the `spec/requests` directory, and some serious opportunities for optimization have presented themselves. First, the initial observation: the `'with API authentication'` context is *exclusively* used in `spec/requests/`, in 71 files, and only 9 of them override the `let(:user)` definition.

The key is in `spec/support/api_authentication.rb`. My thinking is that the repeated instantiation of user objects and tokens is a major bottleneck. The current implementation utilizes `let_it_be` to create a `default_api_user` and `default_api_token`. This approach is good; `let_it_be` would run before each example only once, but there is a risk of a clash if the user is overridden in other specs, leading to an issue with context. This suggests a few strategies:

1.  **Refactoring `api_authentication.rb`:** Consider passing a `user_fabricator` argument to the shared context, allowing for flexibility and preventing unintentional side effects, also it can be improved with something like `user&.id == default_api_user.id` to prevent `WrongScopeError`. This will help determine how we can test the `user` object in contexts like `default_api_token`.
2.  **Optimizing `forbidden for wrong role`:** The `it_behaves_like 'forbidden for wrong role'` example, called 73 times, currently fabricates a new user in each run. This is redundant. A better approach might be to either reuse an existing user or, at least, update a user's role instead of creating a new one. I need to weigh the time saved against the risk of unexpected side effects, but it looks promising.
3.  **Broad Systemic Analysis:** Before making any changes to `api_authentication.rb` and `forbidden for wrong role`, I need a clearer picture of what else is contributing to the runtime. My hunch is that while fabricating users is expensive, there are likely other performance drains.

To get that global view, I'm going to rerun the tests with `TEST_STACK_PROF`, `FPROF`, and `RD_PROF` enabled, focusing on `spec/requests`. This will pinpoint the true bottlenecks now that the Sidekiq `:inline` issue is addressed. Okay, so I've been looking at some test code and have a few immediate thoughts. First, that `profiles_spec.rb` is screaming for attention! Processing those image fixtures with libvips/ImageMagick eight times in a single test at 142ms each is brutal. That adds up to over a second of processing time which is a definite bottleneck. We'll be converting `account` to `let_it_be(:account, refind: true)` in Tier 2 to help with performance, but we need to watch out for file deletion in those DELETE avatar/header tests – gotta ensure those Paperclip files are getting nuked from orbit.

Now, let's switch gears and dig into `api_authentication.rb`. I'm seeing a lot of cleverness here and I need to make sure I understand it. This shared context is used across 71 files, so any changes need to be bulletproof.

The core idea looks solid: It sets up authenticated users and tokens with `let_it_be`, but the `refind: true` option is really throwing some interesting edge cases out there. Let's break it down:

1.  If an example's using `user` with `user.account` the `refind: true` means every example's getting a fresh `User.find(id)` call. This means a fresh DB read inside the example's transaction, avoiding stale data and memoized associations. Excellent.
2.  Now, the `let(:user) { ... }` overrides: If a spec overrides the `user` and the ID doesn't match the default one, the code fabricates a *new* token. If the spec doesn't provide a `user`, the code safely handles the `nil` scenario with the `user&.id` (instead of the original `user.id` that would raise an error). Smart.
3.  Any modifications to the token inside an example (updates, revokes) are effectively isolated. The database transaction handles rollbacks, and since `default_api_token` also has `refind: true`, the next example receives a clean slate. I like this.
4.  But what if we're making assertions on object counts? For the 62 files *not* overriding `let(:user)`, the default user and token are the same across examples. However, if an example skips using the `headers`/`token`/`user` (like an unauthenticated test or a role-based test), we *could* have issues. This is a potential minefield, I've got to run a suite of tests on *all* 71 files to ensure there are no regressions. And I should test multiple random seeds to be absolutely certain.
5.  Wait a sec, I need to zoom out and think about *all* the specs in `/spec/requests/`. Specifically, if any of those tests are using `use_transactional_tests: false` that would totally mess this up. Need to grep for that right now.

Okay, so that's the immediate rundown, I'll start checking the code right now!

First, `Rack::Attack.blocklist('deny from blocklist')` is running on every request. steps.reasoning_content:
**Optimizing Rack::Attack in Request Specs**

Okay, hold on a second... just took a look at `spec/requests/auth/sessions_spec.rb:9` and I see a potential issue with how `Rack::Attack` is handled within our request specs.  The current setup, with the `before { Rack::Attack.enabled = false }` and `after { Rack::Attack.enabled = true }` calls, screams "fragile" to me.

My brain is racing now. If `auth/sessions_spec.rb` re-enables `Rack::Attack` in an `after` hook, and we only disable it globally in a `before(:suite)` hook, we're going to accidentally enable it for *every* subsequent spec! That's a huge potential source of instability and slow test runs.

Here's the plan: I'm thinking we can make this *way* cleaner.  Let's configure `Rack::Attack.enabled = false` in `spec/rails_helper.rb`. Then, for tests that specifically *need* `Rack::Attack` (like, `spec/config/initializers/rack/attack_spec.rb`), we use an `around(:each, :rack_attack)` block. This way, we enable it only for those specific tests, run the example, and ensure it's disabled again afterward. We can mark the test with a `:rack_attack` metadata to flag it appropriately.

Wait, looking more closely at `spec/config/initializers/rack/attack_spec.rb`, I see it's *already* a request spec!  (Line 5: `RSpec.describe Rack::Attack, type: :request do`).  That's perfect!  This means we can apply the `before` hook directly to request specs.

So, in `spec/rails_helper.rb`, let's add this `before` hook:

config.before :each, type: :request do |example|
  # Use https and configured hostname in request spec requests
  integration_session.https!
  host! Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
  Rack::Attack.enabled = !!example.metadata[:rack_attack]
end

And in `spec/config/initializers/rack/attack_spec.rb`, we add `:rack_attack`:

RSpec.describe Rack::Attack, :rack_attack, type: :request do

This way, we can be *sure* to toggle the behavior on a per-spec basis, by utilizing metadata!

Now, the clincher: we need to handle non-request specs (like system specs) correctly. We don't want `auth/sessions_spec.rb` to leak its state. I see a cleaner way:

config.around(:each, type: :request) do |example|
  old_rack_attack = Rack::Attack.enabled
  Rack::Attack.enabled = !!example.metadata[:rack_attack]
  example.run
ensure
  Rack::Attack.enabled = old_rack_attack
end

By storing the *old* value of `Rack::Attack.enabled` and restoring it in the `ensure` block, we guarantee zero side effects across all spec types. That should eliminate any potential leakage. No risk. And we’re saving a significant amount of time, too – ~1.5 seconds and potentially ~2,000 fewer SQL queries in the `spec/requests/` directory.

Okay, let's take this further.  I'm going to scan the *entire* middleware stack in `Rails.application.middleware`. There could be other middleware components that are unnecessarily adding overhead to our request specs, and it's time to find them. I'm going to inspect the time spent in *every* middleware, using a StackProf dump. Time to optimize!

steps.reasoning_content:
**Immediate Performance Bottleneck Investigation**

Okay, hold on a second! This test run took **2 minutes and 14.6 seconds**, while the last one was significantly faster at **1 minute and 46.58 seconds**. That's a huge difference, and I need to figure out why. Let's look at the timing for each spec file:

*   **Previous Run:** `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` took 6.76 seconds, `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` took 5.12 seconds, and `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` took 19.45 seconds.
*   **Current Run:** `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` jumped to 12.7 seconds (almost double!), `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` ran in 7.5 seconds, and `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` took 24.99 seconds.

I see a slowdown across the board, in the range of ~25-40%! This is a serious problem. There are two potential areas I can think of:

1.  **CPU contention:** Is there increased CPU usage on the container host? Maybe other processes are using too many resources.
2.  **`api_authentication.rb` issue:** Did something in `let_it_be` inside `api_authentication.rb` cause PostgreSQL savepoints or `before_all` transactions to linger? Or, potentially, a `user` was created in `:inline` mode.

I'm going to focus on hypothesis #2 first, because that seems more likely. Let's check `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` because its timing jumped the most! The spec went from 6.76 seconds to 12.7 seconds - an 88% increase. However, `cache_spec.rb` which *doesn't* use `api_authentication.rb`, still increased from 19.45 seconds to 24.99 seconds - a 28% increase. This means *something else* is going on.

Why did `v2/notifications_spec.rb` increase so much more than `cache_spec.rb`? Let's investigate this.

I'm going to test *both* of the current hypotheses. I'll start by checking if `before_all` in `api_authentication.rb` leaked a transaction or left `Sidekiq.testing!` in `:inline` mode. Let's run `v2/notifications_spec.rb` and `cache_spec.rb` individually with `EVENT_PROF="sidekiq.inline"` and check `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.open_transactions`. That should point us in the right direction.

steps.message: Let's update `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb` so test routes are drawn once in `before(:all)` and reloaded once in `after(:all)` instead of 30 times, then benchmark it and verify routes remain intact for subsequent specs.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Refactoring `signature_verification_spec.rb` for Efficiency**

Wow, this `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb` is remarkably clean! I see an immediate opportunity to optimize it. First, I'm going to move the `Rails.application.routes.draw do ... end` block into `before(:all)` and pair it with `after(:all) { Rails.application.reload_routes! }`. Hold on, I need to keep the `before { stub_const('ActivityPub::TestsController', activitypub_tests_controller); travel_to '2023-12-20T10:00:00Z' }` block per example since `stub_const` and `travel_to` are handled by RSpec and ActiveSupport. But, I need to check something... what happens if another spec runs *after* this one? The `after(:all)` block and `reload_routes!` should cleanly restore *all* routes after the test.

Wait, instead of `draw` and `reload_routes!`, could I just use `routes.append`? No, that wouldn't work. `routes.append` would leave the test routes appended unless I still called `reload_routes!` in the `after(:all)` block. So, sticking with `before(:all)` with `routes.draw` and `after(:all)` with `reload_routes!` saves a massive amount of time! Checking the time, reloading takes ~0.20 seconds, and this saves 7.2 seconds!

Next, I'll convert the `let_it_be(:actor_keypair)` to a `let_it_be` since it's an OpenSSL::PKey object. BUT!! This test has a tricky bit in line 74! I see `let_it_be(:actor, refind: true)` here, but line 139 overrides this with a different `public_key`! That's because the `username: 'bob', domain: 'remote.domain'` has a UNIQUE index on `(lower(username), lower(domain))`! If line 74 used `let_it_be(:actor)`, line 139 would hit a uniqueness violation! So, I can either keep line 74 as `let!(:actor)` or, inside of line 139, update `actor.update!(public_key: ...)` but the current example setup takes only 0.23 seconds so this is best left untouched. This should make sure `username: 'bob', domain: 'remote.domain'` can be setup in both cases, as is expected. Looking at line 430, `with an HTTP Message Signature (final RFC version)` does *not* override `actor`! So I can safely change that to `let_it_be(:actor, refind: true)`.

Alright, I'm going to apply the `before(:all)` / `after(:all)` route change to `signature_verification_spec.rb` and run some tests right away, including confirming that running another spec right after it ensures the routes are properly restored. Let's see how this goes!

steps.message: Let's refactor the shared thread setup in `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` using `let_it_be` / `before_all` and benchmark it.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Optimizing ActivityPub Replies Spec**

Okay, wow, just looking at `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` is like finding a hidden treasure! This test suite is a major bottleneck. The performance is terrible, and the culprit? Redundant database setup! We're spending **8.39s** (a baseline of **15.94s**) on 45 examples, and a huge chunk of that time is spent creating, again and again, the same database records.

Here's the breakdown: Lines 234-243 in `before` are creating a whole set of data *before* every single example, even for tests that should be quick because of the status' visibility! This means a base `status`, a `bookmark`, two accounts and two users, and *six* more statuses! That's a total of 7 statuses, each resulting in additional model creations. Across 45 examples, that's **315 Statuses and Bookmarks** created just in the `before` block alone. And we also have `10.times` loops generating statuses in the specs themselves, leading to a total of 375 statuses!

The thing is, the `status` record is only varying based on `parent_visibility`: public, private, or direct. So, here's the plan. We need to refactor this setup to create these base objects *once*. Let's introduce `let_it_be` for a `public_status`, `private_status`, `direct_status`, `remote_account`, and `remote_querier`, all with `refind: true`. We can also create the *six* reply statuses within a `before_all` block for the `public_status` (we don't even need to worry about `private` and `direct` if those tests don't actually need them; they are likely to return 404).

Now, what about those `10.times { Fabricate(:status, ...)}` calls? They are adding *more* statuses, and each `Fabricate(:status)` call is creating a new account. The `ActivityPub::RepliesController::DESCENDANTS_LIMIT` is stubbed to 5 anyway, so let's refactor the specs to create as few statuses as possible, by re-using base status instances from the `before_all` block.

But wait! `private` and `direct` statuses: even if we created *one* set of replies for all three visibility statuses *once*, that's only 18 instead of 315! We can even use the same `remote_account` for `private` and `direct` as they're not used in the examples.

Ideally, we could organize the statuses by visibility in a single `let_it_be`:

let_it_be(:remote_account, refind: true) { Fabricate(:account, domain: 'foobar.com') }
let_it_be(:statuses_by_visibility, refind: true) do
  %i(public private direct).index_with do |visibility|
    s = Fabricate(:status, visibility: visibility)
    Fabricate.times(2, :status, thread: s, visibility: :public)
    Fabricate(:status, thread: s, visibility: :private)
    Fabricate(:status, account: s.account, thread: s, visibility: :public)
    Fabricate(:status, account: s.account, thread: s, visibility: :private)
    Fabricate(:status, account: remote_account, thread: s, visibility: :public, uri: "https://foobar.com/statuses/1234-#{visibility}")
    s
  end
let(:status) { statuses_by_visibility.fetch(parent_visibility) }

But, hold on... does `let_it_be` work correctly with a hash of AR objects? No. `refind: true` *only* works for single AR records. So, we'll need separate `let_it_be` calls for each: `public_status`, `private_status`, and `direct_status`, to make sure `refind: true` works correctly.

And, as a final check, accessing `status.account` in each example will always fetch a fresh instance from the database, meaning that changes (like `suspend!`, `mark_deleted!`, `block!`) within an example are properly rolled back at the end of each test.

Let's implement this and benchmark. We should see a dramatic improvement! Remember it took **15.94s at baseline** and **8.3

steps.reasoning_content:
**My Thought Process: Unpacking Performance Bottlenecks**

Okay, the initial results are promising! We've seen a significant speedup with Sidekiq – **15.94s (baseline) dropping to 8.39s (post-Sidekiq), but then approximately ~3.0s** after excluding route load. But wait a second, why is `replies_spec.rb` still taking ~3.0s? That's the real problem to tackle.

Let's dive into the code. Lines 158 and 212 within `shared_examples 'allowed access'` are the likely culprits. This shared example is included three times, so let's focus on these problematic contexts:

*   `context 'when there are many self-replies'`: Ten Fabricated statuses related to the same account are run three times - that's 30 statuses!
*   `context 'when there are many replies'`: Ten Fabricated statuses are run three times, creating 30 statuses, and also 30 accounts + 30 users!.

There's also the `before_all` setup creating 18 statuses. Notably, `private_status` and `direct_status` 404 immediately, so we could theoretically eliminate 12 of those 18 statuses and save time. Wait, but, keeping them only cost 0.2s, whereas those 60 statuses inside `10.times` cost ~2.0s!

Specifically, I'm now zeroing in on line 212: `10.times { Fabricate(:status, thread: status, visibility: :public) }`. The key here is the `only_other_accounts: 'true'` condition - does it *need* 10 DIFFERENT authors? I think not! As it is, reducing the number of these Fabrications has already saved us time. Even without modifying the `10.times` call, going from **15.94s -> 3.0s (5.3x faster!)** is a massive gain. Also, it does not look like we need those 12 extra statuses in `before_all`, for `private_status` and `direct_status`. Wait: what if we check `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` with `--profile 10`? Actually let's move on to #4 and #5 first where there's **~12 MORE SECONDS** waiting!!

---

Okay, now for the bigger fish: `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` (taking `6.76s`–`12.7s`!) and `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` (taking `5.12s`–`7.5s`!). I'm going to read through *both* files completely to translate the `:sidekiq_inline` setups in `before` into a more efficient `before_all` / `let_it_be` strategy. Remember:

*   `v2/notifications_spec.rb` currently executes **404 inline Sidekiq jobs** and runs **11,491 SQL queries**!
*   `v1/notifications_spec.rb` runs **316 inline Sidekiq jobs** and makes **8,745 SQL queries**!

I think it's most productive to read `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` first, and then to consider the v2 version.

steps.message: Let's fix `config.before(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` / `after(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` in `spec/rails_helper.rb` so nested `:sidekiq_inline` groups activate inline mode during `before_all`, fix the nested `before_all` in `v2/notifications_spec.rb`, and use `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)` in `v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb`, then test all 3 specs!
steps.reasoning_content:
**A Deep Dive into RSpec Context and Hook Semantics**

Okay, first reaction: WHOA! That was a tricky one! I need to break down *exactly* why that test failed and, crucially, understand the interplay of RSpec hooks and the `before_all` construct in TestProf.

The initial error was pretty clear: no notifications were being created during the `before_all` block. Why? My first thought was the `config.before(:context)` hook wasn't executing correctly. The issue boiled down to the scope. RSpec's global `config.before(:context)` only runs once *per top-level* example group. If I don't filter it, the nested `describe` blocks don't get the hook, unless explicitly tagged (in our case, `:sidekiq_inline`). Initially, that block had no filtering.

So, the `config.before(:context)` set Sidekiq to `:fake` at the top level, and then the nested `describe` block was executed. The hook *didn't* re-run, because it's global and not filtered, and `before_all` was trying to do something that depended on the Sidekiq setting.

That explains the first error. But there was another! It was related to TestProf's `before_all`. It seems you can't *nest* `before_all` blocks. A `before_all` begins a transaction at the outer scope, and nesting it causes conflicts.

So the plan now is to fix it. I'm going to add `config.before(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` and `config.after(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` to `rails_helper.rb`, and keep the line with nested `before_all` as a regular `before` block.

But there's more... checking `v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` made me look more closely at how the `user` object was being handled inside `before_all`. I noticed a mismatch: `let_it_be` used at the top level and just `let` for a nested one. Inside `before_all`, you can *only* use `let_it_be`!

I'm starting to see a cleaner pattern, especially in `spec/support/api_authentication.rb`. If I can make `user` directly available via `let_it_be` (instead of using a `let` block that references something defined elsewhere), it becomes available in ALL API specs!

But what if a spec *overrides* the `let(:user)`? That's when things get even more interesting. If `include_context` defines a `let_it_be(:user)` *and* the spec defines `let(:user)` *after* the `include_context`, the behavior changes. Because `before_all` is run *at runtime*, the `let(:user)` declaration inside the spec would *override* the previously defined `let_it_be`, resulting in a `WrongScopeError`! The original code was written this way for a *reason*! It's *definitely* necessary to use `let_it_be` in that case, to avoid the issue.

Now the plan is solid: in `api_authentication.rb`, I'll use `let_it_be(:default_api_user)` and `let_it_be(:default_api_token)`. Then, in `v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb`, I'll use `let_it_be(:user)` directly, just as in `v1` and `v2` notification specs.

In short, the failures are because of the RSpec hook's scope plus the nested `before_all`. I'm confident that addressing those in `rails_helper.rb`, `v2/notifications_spec.rb`, and `v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` will resolve everything. It's time to run those three specs and see!

Okay, so the initial analysis on notification specs is in, and the results are pretty damn exciting. It's like, BOOM! I've smashed all three notification specs together, and the performance improvement is massive. The baseline was a cringe-worthy 14.68 seconds (21 seconds under load!), but now, we're talking a breezy 3.86 seconds, which is about 3.4 seconds in the suite – that’s a whopping ~4.3x speed up! It amounts to saving ~11 seconds across those three files. Sweet!

However, I'm still a little puzzled as to why `v2/notifications_spec.rb` is lingering at ~2 seconds. Hmm, looks like "when there are numerous notifications for the same final group" is the culprit. Looks like it calls `FavouriteService.new.call(...)` five times, twice, totaling 1 second of execution. Everything else is negligible!

Alright, time to dig into Batch 2, the next top slowest files pulled from the `RD_PROF` data. I've got my sights set on:

1.  `spec/requests/activitypub/contexts_spec.rb` – clocking in at 2.21 seconds with 7 examples and a hefty 3,116 SQL queries. Ouch!
2.  `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/public_spec.rb` – 2.23 seconds for 12 examples, and I see "media\_status" 12 times. Curious!
3.  `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb` – 1.64 seconds for 11 examples.
4.  `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/tag_spec.rb` – 0.91 seconds for 11 examples.
5.  `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb` – 0.74 seconds for 6 examples.
6.  `spec/requests/api/v1/conversations_spec.rb` – 0.72 seconds for 4 examples.

Time to dive in and get to work on these six files! Let's see what gems we can find in each of them.

steps.message: Let's read `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/public_spec.rb` and `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb`.
steps.reasoning_content:
**A Moment of Insight!**

Okay, hold on a second! I need to stop and really *look* at something. This discrepancy is screaming at me from `spec/requests/activitypub/contexts_spec.rb`! Specifically, lines 77-81 and then lines 121-124... the `GET #show` versus the `GET #items` test.

On line 78, we have this `context 'with many statuses'`, and it's using the default `ActivityPub::ContextsController::DESCENDANTS_LIMIT.times` to fabricate a bunch of statuses. In this case `40`.  Then, just a few lines down (line 122!), the exact same context name, *with many statuses*, but this time the author used `stub_const 'ActivityPub::ContextsController::DESCENDANTS_LIMIT', 2`.

*Aha!* That's it! They stubbed the constant to `2` for `GET #items`, but completely forgot to do it in the `GET #show` test!  This meant the latter was generating the full `DESCENDANTS_LIMIT` of 40 statuses, creating a performance bottleneck of **2.38 seconds** at baseline, and **1.75s** post-Sidekiq, making it the slowest single example in all of `spec/requests`!! That's a ridiculous amount of overhead, especially considering all the associated database lookups and object creation that goes along with those statuses: **40 Bookmarks + 80 Accounts + 80 Users + 80 BCrypt hashes + 160 LoginActivities!**

So, the fix is straightforward:  We need to add `stub_const 'ActivityPub::ContextsController::DESCENDANTS_LIMIT', 2` to the `GET #show`'s 'with many statuses' block, matching how it's done in `GET #items`. Plus, we should also include a `let_it_be(:conversation, refind: true)`. This should cut the runtime of `activitypub/contexts_spec.rb` from **2.47 seconds** down to a lightning-fast **~0.15 seconds**, a 16x speed improvement!

Now, let's also take a look at `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/public_spec.rb` and `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb` to see if we can find similar issues and apply what we've learned!

**My Eureka Moment: Two Crystal-Clear Lessons!**

Okay, two glaring issues just jumped out at me, and I see the path forward to fix them. Let's break this down:

First, **`profiles_spec.rb:172`**: The Paperclip debacle. Right, `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` triggers `account.avatar = nil; account.save!`, which then calls `flush_deletes` *before* the commit. This means the avatar file is being deleted prematurely in `spec/test_files/`. The solution is to isolate the destructive behavior. I need to keep `let_it_be(:account, refind: true)` for the majority of the tests where we're *not* deleting. For the two cases that *do* delete (`DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` and `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header`), I should either use a fresh `let(:account)` *only* within those specific contexts, override `let(:account)` within those `describe` blocks. Actually, since only those two endpoints have delete functionality, creating a fresh `let(:account)` there is the most efficient solution: (2 + 2 = 4 instead of 8). It's all about scoping the destructive actions appropriately. Let's see if the lines 135-190 of `profiles_spec.rb` offer any further insight.

Second, **`statuses_spec.rb:155, 211, 230, 268, 286`** (all within `when signed in`): This one is more immediate. Why are these tests failing within this context? Line 147 is the key: `before { sign_in_with_session(user) }`. My guess is that the issue lies within `sign_in_with_session`. It's likely using `let(:user)`, `SessionActivation`, or `user.password`, and something there is causing the problem. Let's dive into the implementation of `sign_in_with_session` at the bottom of `statuses_spec.rb` and get to the root of that problem.

steps.message: Let's check lines 59-136 of `spec/requests/api/v1/profiles_spec.rb` to ensure `PATCH /api/v1/profile` doesn't touch avatar/header files on disk.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Eureka! Optimization Found!**

Okay, I've got it! That `statuses_spec.rb` file was giving me a headache. Line 321, specifically. The problem was right there: `post user_session_path, params: { user: { email: user.email, password: user.password } }`. Using `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)` to refind the user from PostgreSQL was setting `user.password` to `nil`. Obviously, `user.password` is a virtual attribute, not a database column. The simple fix, as usual, is `let_it_be(:user, reload: true) { Fabricate(:user) }`. Now the Ruby object is preserved, and the password stays intact while reloading the database attributes. I'll document that as Gotcha #5 in `docs/test_suite_optimization.md`: `refind: true` clears Devise's in-memory password!

Now, onto `profiles_spec.rb`. The `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header` failing after `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` was a clue. `account.avatar.exists?` checks `File.exist?` on disk, not the DB. The avatar delete in the second spec was calling `account.avatar.destroy` -> `account.save`, which triggers `after_save` -> `flush_deletes` to remove the image file from disk. The solution is simple! Only those two `DELETE` examples delete files on disk, while the rest are fine. Let's optimize.

If I use `let_it_be(:account, refind: true)` for the `GET /api/v1/profile`, `PATCH /api/v1/profile`, and the `with wrong scope` examples, leaving the `DELETE` examples with fresh accounts, it cuts down on the image processing by about 62%! The cleanest way seems to be to put `context 'with valid scope'` around the `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` examples. It reduces the number of image uploads from 8 to 3!

And I should check the `PATCH /api/v1/profile` spec too to ensure it's not also overwriting the avatar or header, just to be sure.

steps.reasoning_content:
**Refactoring the `profiles_spec.rb` Test Suite**

Aha! Let's dive into this `profiles_spec.rb` file. I see that the `PATCH /api/v1/profile` endpoint is responsible for uploading new avatars and headers, effectively replacing them on disk. That's good to know. Now, a key observation: the tests for `PATCH /api/v1/profile` don't even *require* the account to have existing avatars or headers *before* the request. Even failures like "forbidden for wrong scope" and "with invalid data" don't depend on the pre-existence of these media files! However, `GET /api/v1/profile` and `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` & `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header` do seem to *require* pre-existing files for the `account`.

Thinking through this, I can clean things up:

My initial thought is to keep the top-level `let_it_be(:account, refind: true) { Fabricate(:account) }` *without* any avatar/header attachments. Then, in the `GET`, and `DELETE` success examples, I can attach the necessary media. No, wait, even the `DELETE` with wrong-scope doesn't care. Also, the `PATCH` upload doesn't check for prior media attachments!

Now, does a successful `PATCH /api/v1/profile` implicitly rely on the `account` existing? Yes, it does exist, given the existing `let_it_be` definition. But, ONLY `GET /api/v1/profile`, `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar`, and `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header` actually need those `avatar` and `header` attachments.

To verify this, I'll go through the spec. For the `GET /api/v1/profile` examples, I can either attach the avatar/header in the `GET` examples, or leverage the top-level. The same holds true for the `DELETE` endpoints, attaching in the success examples.

Here's an even simpler approach: a helper, or just use:
*   At the top-level, define `let_it_be(:default_account, refind: true) { Fabricate(:account) }` and `let(:account) { default_account }`.

*   Then, in only the examples where they're *absolutely* needed - in `GET /api/v1/profile`, `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` (success), and `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header` (success) - I'll override `let(:account)` with a `Fabricate(:account, avatar: ..., header: ...)` call. Wait, in `GET /api/v1/profile` and `DELETE` wrong-scope, no media files are mutated! So the top-level `let_it_be` with no media works for all non-deleting examples. BUT...

I need to account for what happens during the `PATCH` call. When I upload a new `avatar.gif` and `attachment.jpg`, Paperclip writes new files with *new* hashes. Also, it deletes the old files on disk! This means `PATCH` *also* deletes old avatar/header files if the filenames differ!

Therefore, the best approach is to have a lightweight `let_it_be(:account, refind: true) { Fabricate(:account) }` at the top level (no images). Then, *only* in the `GET /api/v1/profile`, `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` (success), and `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header` (success) examples do I need to define `let(:account) { Fabricate(:account, avatar: ..., header: ...) }`. This approach offers these advantages:

*   It makes the file system 100% safe, regardless of test execution order.
*   It significantly reduces the number of heavy image uploads from 8 to just 3! (and for `PATCH`, it avoids uploading 2 images just to throw them away!)

I'll apply this change, along with the `statuses_spec.rb` `reload: true` fix, and then test all 4 files across 3 seeds to ensure everything is stable.

     - `spec/requests/api/v1/statuses/favourites_spec.rb` (`POST .../unfavourite`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/conversations_spec.rb` (`GET /api/v1/conversations`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb` (`when the timeline is available`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` (`GET /unread_count`, `GET /notifications`)

2. **Setup-level optimizations in slow request specs:**
   - `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` (`27.65s` -> `~3.7s`)
   - `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` (`15.94s` -> `~2.3–3.0s`)
   - `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb` (`7.65s` -> `~0.7s`, routes drawn/reloaded once via `before(:all)` / `after(:all)`)
   - `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` (`8.20s` -> `~1.9s`), `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` (`5.68s` -> `~1.1s`), `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` (`0.80s` -> `~0.3s`)

   - `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/{public,link,tag,home,list}_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/conversations_spec.rb`
   - `spec/requests/accounts_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/statuses_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/statuses/activity_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/activitypub/{outboxes,collections}_spec.rb`

   - `spec/requests/api/v1/admin/{accounts,reports,account_actions,canonical_email_blocks}_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`
   - `spec/requests/api/v1/{accounts,statuses,collections,follow_requests}_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/accounts/{statuses,following_accounts,follower_accounts}_spec.rb`
   - `spec/requests/api/v1/statuses/{quotes,favourites,bookmarks,pins,reblogs,mutes,sources,translations,interaction_policies,favourited_by_accounts,reblogged_by_accounts}_spec.rb`
   - `spec/requests/api/v1/lists/accounts_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications/{requests,policies}_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications/policies_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/filters/{keywords,statuses}_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/search_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/web/embeds_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/announcements/reactions_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/emails/confirmations_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/instances/domain_blocks_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v1/push/subscriptions_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/oauth/userinfo_spec.rb`

### Phase 2 Results (`spec/requests`)

| Metric | Baseline (post-Phase 1) | After Tier 1A (`Sidekiq :fake`) | Final (Tier 1 + Tier 2) | Total Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wall time (seed `15045`) | `151.6s` | `106.58s` (`-29.7%`) | `49.14s` | **-67.6% (3.09x faster)** |
| Wall time (avg of 3 seeds) | `151.6s` | `106.58s` | `48.52s` (`47.6s–49.1s`) | **-68.0% (3.12x faster)** |
| User CPU time | `130.7s` | `91.6s` | `42.3s` (`41.4s–43.1s`) | **-67.6%** |
| Setup time (`RD_PROF=1`) | `158.7s` | `89.5s` | `22.1s` | **-86.1%** |
| Fabricated objects (`FPROF=1`) | `~11,030` (`~115s+`) | `11,030` (`68.8s`) | `3,161` (`19.3s`) | **-71.3% objects** |
| SQL queries (`sql.active_record`) | `~250k+` | `167,811` (`22.65s`) | `71,025` (`8.59s`) | **-57.7% vs Tier 1A** |
| Inline Sidekiq jobs | `~5,000+` (`~46s`) | `929` (`10.40s`) | `206` (`2.07s`) | **-95%+ vs baseline** |
| Failures | `0` / 1,877 | `0` / 1,877 | `0` / 1,877 | Maintained |

### Combined Progress (`spec/models` + `spec/requests`)

- **Combined baseline:** `120.2s` (`spec/models`) + `>151.6s` (`spec/requests`) = **`>271.8s`**
- **Combined after Phase 1 + Phase 2:** `~32–45s` (`spec/models`) + `~48.5s` (`spec/requests`) = **`~80–94s`** (**~3.0x–3.4x faster**, exceeding the 2x goal before even touching factories!)

### Additional Mastodon-Specific Gotchas Discovered in Phase 2

5. **Nested `:sidekiq_inline` groups with `before_all`:**
   - An unfiltered `config.before(:context)` only executes at the top-level `RSpec.describe`, NOT when entering a nested `describe`/`context` tagged `:sidekiq_inline`. Dedicated `config.before(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` and `config.after(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` hooks are required so `before_all` inside nested `:sidekiq_inline` groups runs in `:inline` mode.
6. **Devise in-memory `user.password` with `refind: true`:**
   - `refind: true` reloads the `User` via `User.find(id)`, losing the in-memory virtual `password` attribute (e.g., `sign_in_with_session` in `spec/requests/statuses_spec.rb` posts `user.password`). Use `reload: true` instead of `refind: true` when an example reads `user.password`.
7. **Paperclip file deletion on disk inside rolled-back transactions:**
   - Deleting or replacing an attachment (`DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar`, `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header`, `PATCH /api/v1/profile`) triggers Paperclip\x27s `flush_deletes` on disk in `after_save` even though the DB transaction rolls back, causing later examples checking `expect(account.avatar).to exist` to fail if they share the same `let_it_be` attachment. Keep destructive attachment tests on a per-example fabricated record while sharing lightweight records elsewhere.
8. **Snowflake ID creation order in pagination assertions:**
   - Mastodon\x27s Snowflake IDs increase monotonically with creation order. When converting `let` / `let!` declarations to `let_it_be`, preserve the relative creation order of records referenced by `min_id` / `max_id` pagination headers (e.g., `remote_status` before `local_status` in `link_spec.rb`, `pending_account` before `admin_account` in `v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`).

---

## Plan for Future Phases

### Phase 3: Fabricators (`spec/fabricators/`) — Do Not Touch Until Factories Phase

Profiling `spec/models` and `spec/requests` uncovered massive hidden cascades inside `spec/fabricators/` that affect **all** spec types:

1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb:11` (HUGE):**
   ```ruby
   after_create do |status|
     Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status)
   end
   ```
   - Every `Fabricate(:status)` creates an unexpected `Bookmark`, which via `bookmark_fabricator.rb` builds a brand-new `Account` -> builds a brand-new `User` -> hashes a BCrypt password -> creates 2 `LoginActivity` rows!
   - Even after Phase 1 & Phase 2 `let_it_be` reductions, `bookmark` still accounted for `449` calls (`5.41s`, ~19% of factory time) in `spec/models` and `295` calls (`3.14s`, ~16% of factory time, only 9 top-level!) in `spec/requests`.
   - Removing this implicit `after_create` (and adding explicit `Fabricate(:bookmark)` only in the few specs that actually expect a bookmark) will yield another huge suite-wide speedup.

2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb:17`:**
   ```ruby
   after_create do |user|
     2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) }
   end
   ```
   - Creates 2 `LoginActivity` rows for every fabricated `User` (including every local `Account`!). Still `692` calls in `spec/requests` even after Phase 2. Most specs never inspect `login_activities`.

3. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb:11` (BCrypt hashing):**
   - `password '123456789'` runs `BCrypt::Password.create` (cost 4) on every fabricated `User` / local `Account` (~3.3s in `spec/models` at baseline; ~5s in `spec/requests` at baseline!).
   - Precomputing a single static `Devise::Encryptor.digest(User, '123456789')` and assigning `encrypted_password` directly (unless `:password` is explicitly passed) will eliminate almost all BCrypt CPU time across the entire suite.

4. **`spec/fabricators/account_fabricator.rb:14`:**
   - `user { |attrs| attrs[:domain].nil? ? Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }` builds and persists a full `User` for every local `Account`. Audit whether local accounts always need a `User` or if a lightweight trait / lazy association is feasible.

5. **Remaining `spec/requests` fabrications (`spec/requests/admin/*`):**
   - After Phase 2, `admin_user` still accounts for `89` calls (`1.06s`) across ~40 small `spec/requests/admin/*_spec.rb` files doing `before { sign_in Fabricate(:admin_user) }`. Optimizing `user_fabricator` (BCrypt + `login_activity`) in Phase 3 will automatically slash all of these without needing to edit 40 tiny files.
MARKDOWN

   - Sharing `default_api_user` and `default_api_token` per example group via `let_it_be(..., refind: true)` (falling back cleanly when `user` or `scopes` is overridden, and updating `default_api_user`'s `role` inside the example transaction for `forbidden for wrong role`) eliminates hundreds of `User`/`AdminUser`/`AccessToken` fabrications across the entire API request suite.
3. **Unnecessary `Rack::Attack` execution on all 1,944 test HTTP requests (~1.5s + ~2,000+ SQL queries):**
   - Only `spec/config/initializers/rack/attack_spec.rb` tests `Rack::Attack`. Disabling `Rack::Attack` by default for `type: :request` in `spec/rails_helper.rb` (with opt-in `:rack_attack` tag on `attack_spec.rb`) eliminates per-request `IpBlock.blocked?` queries, duplicate token lookups, and 21 throttle checks while restoring the prior state in `ensure`.
4. **Full Rails route table reloaded 30 times in `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb` (~7.3s):**
   - Drawing test routes once in `before(:all)` and reloading routes once in `after(:all)` (while keeping `stub_const` and `travel_to` per-example) cuts `signature_verification_spec.rb` from `7.65s` down to `~0.7s`.
5. **Repeated heavy setup in slow request specs (`before_all` / `let_it_be`):**
   - `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` recreated 7 records (including 2 statuses, moderator user, invite, poll, token) 258 times (`27.65s` -> `~3.7s`).
   - `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` recreated a 7-status thread 45 times (`15.94s` -> `~2.3–3.0s`).
   - `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` & `v1/notifications_spec.rb` & `v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` ran `PostStatusService`/`FavouriteService`/`ReblogService`/`FollowService` with inline Sidekiq on every read-only `GET` example (`14.7s` combined -> `~3.0s`).
   - `spec/requests/activitypub/contexts_spec.rb` fabricated 40 statuses (`DESCENDANTS_LIMIT`) in `GET #show` even though `GET #items` in the same file already stubbed `DESCENDANTS_LIMIT` to `2` (`3.29s` -> `~0.47s`).
   - Plus `let_it_be`/`before_all` & shared `'with API authentication'` adoption in the next ~40 setup-heavy request specs (timelines, accounts, statuses, profiles, outboxes, admin accounts/reports/account_actions/canonical_email_blocks, media, quotes, favourites, bookmarks, pins, filters, search, lists, collections, embeds, etc.).

### Changes Applied in Phase 2

1. **Systemic / Configuration-level & Shared-setup changes:**
   - Extended `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` default in `spec/rails_helper.rb` to `%i(model request)` and added `config.before(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` / `config.after(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` hooks so nested `:sidekiq_inline` groups run `before_all` in `:inline` mode and cleanly restore `:fake` afterward.
   - Tagged the 9 request spec files requiring inline Sidekiq execution with `:sidekiq_inline` at the minimal context/example scope:
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/admin/account_actions_spec.rb` (`a successful notification delivery`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/reports_spec.rb` (`it 'creates a report'`)
     - `spec/requests/admin/confirmations_spec.rb` (`it 'does not resend confirmation mail'` — ensures negative assertion is not vacuous)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/statuses/favourites_spec.rb` (`POST .../unfavourite`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/conversations_spec.rb` (`GET /api/v1/conversations`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb` (`when the timeline is available`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` (`GET /unread_count`, `GET /notifications`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` (`GET /unread_count`, `GET /notifications`)
     - `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` (`GET .../accounts`)
   - Disabled `Rack::Attack` by default for `type: :request` in `spec/rails_helper.rb` via `around(:each, type: :request)` (opt-in `:rack_attack` tag), and tagged `spec/config/initializers/rack/attack_spec.rb` with `:rack_attack`.
   - Updated `spec/support/api_authentication.rb` to share `default_api_user` and `default_api_token` per example group via `let_it_be(..., refind: true)` (with optional `user_fabricator: nil` for specs defining custom users, and automatic fallback when `user` or `scopes` is overridden).
   - Updated `spec/support/examples/api.rb` (`forbidden for wrong role`) to reuse `default_api_user` with an in-transaction `update!(role:)` when available instead of fabricating a new user 73 times.

2. **Setup-level optimizations in slow request specs:**
   - `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` (`27.65s` -> `~3.7s`)
   - `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` (`15.94s` -> `~2.3–3.0s`)

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wall time (seed `15045`) | `151.6s` | `106.58s` (`-29.7%`) | `49.14s` | **-67.6% (3.09x faster)** |

### Combined Progress (`spec/models` + `spec/requests`)

- **Combined baseline:** `120.2s` (`spec/models`) + `>151.6s` (`spec/requests`) = **`>271.8s`**
- **Combined after Phase 1 + Phase 2:** `~32–45s` (`spec/models`) + `~48.5s` (`spec/requests`) = **`~80–94s`** (**~3.0x–3.4x faster**, exceeding the 2x goal before even touching factories!)

### Additional Mastodon-Specific Gotchas Discovered in Phase 2

5. **Nested `:sidekiq_inline` groups with `before_all`:**
   - An unfiltered `config.before(:context)` only executes at the top-level `RSpec.describe`, NOT when entering a nested `describe`/`context` tagged `:sidekiq_inline`. Dedicated `config.before(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` and `config.after(:context, :sidekiq_inline)` hooks are required so `before_all` inside nested `:sidekiq_inline` groups runs in `:inline` mode.
6. **Devise in-memory `user.password` with `refind: true`:**
   - `refind: true` reloads the `User` via `User.find(id)`, losing the in-memory virtual `password` attribute (e.g., `sign_in_with_session` in `spec/requests/statuses_spec.rb` posts `user.password`). Use `reload: true` instead of `refind: true` when an example reads `user.password`.
7. **Paperclip file deletion on disk inside rolled-back transactions:**
   - Deleting or replacing an attachment (`DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar`, `DELETE /api/v1/profile/header`, `PATCH /api/v1/profile`) triggers Paperclip's `flush_deletes` on disk in `after_save` even though the DB transaction rolls back, causing later examples checking `expect(account.avatar).to exist` to fail if they share the same `let_it_be` attachment. Keep destructive attachment tests on a per-example fabricated record while sharing lightweight records elsewhere.
8. **Snowflake ID creation order in pagination assertions:**
   - Mastodon's Snowflake IDs increase monotonically with creation order. When converting `let` / `let!` declarations to `let_it_be`, preserve the relative creation order of records referenced by `min_id` / `max_id` pagination headers (e.g., `remote_status` before `local_status` in `link_spec.rb`, `pending_account` before `admin_account` in `v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`).

---

## Plan for Future Phases

### Phase 3: Fabricators (`spec/fabricators/`) — Do Not Touch Until Factories Phase

Profiling `spec/models` and `spec/requests` uncovered massive hidden cascades inside `spec/fabricators/` that affect **all** spec types:

1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb:11` (HUGE):**
   ```ruby
   after_create do |status|
     Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status)
   end
   ```
   - Every `Fabricate(:status)` creates an unexpected `Bookmark`, which via `bookmark_fabricator.rb` builds a brand-new `Account` -> builds a brand-new `User` -> hashes a BCrypt password -> creates 2 `LoginActivity` rows!
   - Even after Phase 1 & Phase 2 `let_it_be` reductions, `bookmark` still accounted for `449` calls (`5.41s`, ~19% of factory time) in `spec/models` and `295` calls (`3.14s`, ~16% of factory time, only 9 top-level!) in `spec/requests`.
   - Removing this implicit `after_create` (and adding explicit `Fabricate(:bookmark)` only in the few specs that actually expect a bookmark) will yield another huge suite-wide speedup.

2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb:17`:**
   ```ruby
   after_create do |user|
     2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) }
   end
   ```
   - Creates 2 `LoginActivity` rows for every fabricated `User` (including every local `Account`!). Still `692` calls in `spec/requests` even after Phase 2. Most specs never inspect `login_activities`.

3. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb:11` (BCrypt hashing):**
   - `password '123456789'` runs `BCrypt::Password.create` (cost 4) on every fabricated `User` / local `Account` (~3.3s in `spec/models` at baseline; ~5s in `spec/requests` at baseline!).
   - Precomputing a single static `Devise::Encryptor.digest(User, '123456789')` and assigning `encrypted_password` directly (unless `:password` is explicitly passed) will eliminate almost all BCrypt CPU time across the entire suite.

4. **`spec/fabricators/account_fabricator.rb:14`:**
   - `user { |attrs| attrs[:domain].nil? ? Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }` builds and persists a full `User` for every local `Account`. Audit whether local accounts always need a `User` or if a lightweight trait / lazy association is feasible.

5. **Remaining `spec/requests` fabrications (`spec/requests/admin/*`):**
   - After Phase 2, `admin_user` still accounts for `89` calls (`1.06s`) across ~40 small `spec/requests/admin/*_spec.rb` files doing `before { sign_in Fabricate(:admin_user) }`. Optimizing `user_fabricator` (BCrypt + `login_activity`) in Phase 3 will automatically slash all of these without needing to edit 40 tiny files.
